title: Swedish Empire
capsule: The Swedish Empire (Stormaktstiden, 'Age of Greatness') was forged through a series of wars beginning with Gustavus Adolphus's entry into the Thirty Years' War in 1630, which established Sweden as a major Protestant power and, by the Peace of Westphalia (1648), awarded it substantial territories in northern Germany including Swedish Pomerania and the mouths of the Oder, Elbe, and Weser. Sweden dominated the Baltic after the Peace of Roskilde (1658) forced Denmark to cede Scania and Blekinge, making the Baltic effectively a Swedish lake. The empire collapsed rapidly after Charles XII's defeat at Poltava (1709); the Great Northern War ended with the Peace of Nystad (1721), by which Sweden ceded the eastern Baltic provinces to Russia, and the final collapse of great-power status came with the loss of Finland to Russia in 1809.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Swedish imperial boundaries are well-documented through the series of peace treaties (Westphalia 1648, Roskilde 1658, Nystad 1721) and Swedish administrative records. The extent of Swedish overlordship in northern Germany and the eastern Baltic is treaty-defined and reliable; frontier zones in Norway and northern Scandinavia are less precisely delimited.
